item.title: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
item.description:
US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer.

Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models."

"This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post . "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model."

It doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea . And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act.

On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday said it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and currently under investigation by the FBI.

Whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China."

These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz said its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed.

How DePue reached his conclusion

The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs.

As described in the report, model weights – the parameters that change in relation to training data – must be initialized with some value. One method for doing so involves a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox. The algorithm starts with a seed value that produces the same set of initial values whenever it's run.

Using PyTorch, initialization can be done by creating multiple GPU threads that work in parallel, with the help of Nvidia's cuRAND library. And because this process is not truly random, it's possible to select a chip and a seed value, generate the initial weights for that hardware and compare that pattern to a model's published weights.

"I searched more than six trillion combinations of chip layout and seed number and matched them to open-weights models," said DePue. "In doing so, I found conclusive evidence that six Chinese AI models – including DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, and MiniMax-M3 – were initialized on Nvidia Blackwell systems. Four of the models match Grace Blackwell, the GB200 and GB300 parts in Nvidia's flagship liquid-cooled rack-scale systems."

Noting that this is the first time MiniMax and Ant Group have been publicly linked to usage of Nvidia's Blackwell, he also cited several limitations to his approach. One is that usage of Blackwell GPUs doesn't prove where the GPUs were located, so it's possible some of these Chinese labs used this hardware through US providers – a loophole the Cloud Security Act aims to close.

DePue's report includes initial seed values that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Nvidia's Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, for those who wish to attempt to reproduce the results. DuPue claims that multiple senior researchers, both independent and inside frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, have confirmed the result.

Coincidentally, OpenAI and Anthropic have each complained about Chinese labs copying their models through distillation, a pastime also noted by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. ®

item.title: This year’s bug count just passed 100K
item.description:
Chalk up a new record for vulns. The number of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) found and disclosed so far in 2026 surpassed 100,000 on Friday - more than double 2025’s total - and the reason can be summed up in two letters: AI.

“It’s kind of wild,” Josh Bressers, VulnCheck’s director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure, told The Register . “The thing that almost scares the bejesus out of me is while 100K sounds like a lot, in a couple years we're going to say, remember when it was only 100K?”

As of the time of our interview, about 4 pm UTC on Friday, VulnCheck counted 100,222 CVEs, he said. Microsoft alone added 1,094 security flaws to the total count on Tuesday, following 1,474 vulnerabilities the month before.

“There's no denying the fact that vulnerability hunting with AI is driving a majority of what we're seeing.” All the major CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) - these are the organizations authorized by the CVE program to assign unique identifiers to security vulnerabilities - like VulnCheck, Microsoft, Oracle, GitHub, and other large enterprise IT vendors “are just screaming into the atmosphere right now,” Bressers said. “It’s AI.”

Meanwhile, the percentage of these bugs that are exploited in the wild remains relatively consistent. About 1.4 percent (1,363) of the CVEs published this year have been added to VulnCheck’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

“But obviously, as the number of CVEs grows, [1 percent] of 1,000 is a lot different than [1 percent] of 100,000,” Bressers said.

Plus, as other security researchers have documented, the window between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits – often by reverse engineering the patch while end users are still applying the fix – is rapidly shrinking. This is also thanks to AI .

From CVE to KEV

From January to June, 88 percent of the exploitation observed by CrowdStrike using public proof-of-concept (PoC) code occurred within 48 hours of the code's release. The security firm said China-linked groups such as Vault Panda and Genesis Panda moved even faster, launching attacks within 24 hours of disclosure.

Similarly, VulnCheck found the median time from CVE publication to exploitation falling from 120 days in 2025 to 80 days during the first half of 2026. This window has closed even further during the second half of the year, which also seems to coincide with the AI-induced vulnpocalypse .

“It’s often just hours,” Bressers said, noting 14 make-me-root vulnerabilities that VulnCheck disclosed on Friday in Copeland refrigeration controllers. Two are under active exploitation. These are the devices that Iranian hackers abused to spoil food and spark fires in supermarkets across Europe .

“We published those CVEs, and literally minutes later, we were seeing hits on our honey pots,” Bressers said about the Copeland device vulnerabilities. “We’ve hit a point where with anything that looks interesting, someone is taking that information and seeing what they can do with it. Is it AI driven? Probably. It'd be hard to say it's not, because we've seen it really ramp up recently.”

This influx of software bugs requires a sea change in how the entire industry approaches vulnerability disclosure and patching.

“We don't have a security problem anymore,” Bressers said. “We have a data problem now. Instead of obsessing over vulnerabilities, we need to start looking at things like heat maps for infrastructure, and figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you. The CISA BOD helps with that.”

What to prioritize in a patchpocalypse

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) in June issued a cybersecurity directive that replaces flat-deadline vulnerability management policies. Instead of prioritizing patching based solely on CVSS severity scores, the directive instructs organizations to prioritize based on specific risk criteria, including whether the asset is internet-exposed, under active exploitation, and whether an attacker can automate the exploit.

“It's telling people to figure out the vulnerabilities that actually affect you, and then put those at the top of the list, instead of just saying we're going to fix all the criticals,” Bressers said.

AI-generated vulnerability disclosures also create huge headaches for open source software developers and maintainers, which Bressers describes as a security problem “ super close to my heart .”

“You've got individual developers that are drowning in vulnerability reports,” he said. “You have foundations being crushed by AI agents scraping their data or downloading their packages, millions of times a day, and it's straining the seams absolutely everywhere you look. The one thing I can say with certainty is: The way we currently do things has to change, and it's going to have to change fairly soon.”

Different open source projects have taken different approaches to solving this issue. The Eclipse Foundation, which houses the Open VSX Registry , in April launched a “managed tier” for enterprise customers and other organizations running Open VSX at scale.

Instead of using the free, open source version, the managed version guarantees a 99.95 percent uptime SLA backed by service credits. Its customers include AWS, IBM, Google, Cursor, and Windsurf. This paid option means commercial users who rely on the registry help fund its ongoing maintenance - and their own platforms’ security and performance.

Meanwhile, curl’s maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, citing an “ avalanche of vulnerability reports ," updated its bug reporting rules last month. As of October 26, all low- and medium-severity reports go directly into the public GitHub repository, with only the high- and critical-flaws receiving private handling.

Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty program this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team.

“A lot more needs to happen, and I think it is going to be a challenge to enact some of this change,”  Bressers said. “When a package registry drastically changes something, people start freaking out, and the world is going to end, and people on LinkedIn are complaining - a lot of people are hesitant. No one wants to be the first to jump into the alligator-filled pool. That's one of our challenges.”®

item.title: Meatbags suck at spotting lying LLMs, so let AI narc on itself
item.description:
The internet is full of schlock, from biased news and dubious hot takes to false factoids. LogicLens aims to separate fact from fiction using the very same technology behind some of that slop: AI.

It’s a simple premise, really: LogicLens, which lives in Chrome as a browser extension , or on iOS in the form of a mobile app called Receipts , combs through articles, social media posts, and other content to check it not only for factual inaccuracies, but also for bad reasoning. LogicLens and Receipts claim to identify logical fallacies , flag reports that misrepresent information, detect content that attempts to polarize an issue, and the like.

It also cites sources, so if, for example, you need to call someone out on their BS, you’ll have ammunition. Or, if you’re trying to fact-check something before sharing it, you can get a more accurate view of the situation, and maybe post something else instead.

Using the Chrome extension is as simple as clicking on its icon in the list of extensions in the browser. On iOS, the Receipts app is found as a share option. Once it starts, LogicLens scans an article, post, video, etc. to find potential issues of factual or logical inconsistency and flags them for review.

If the facts of the matter turn out to contradict your worldview, LogicLens’ creators say they’re not trying to be partisan - you may just not be as informed as you need to be, which hopefully their tool will assist with.

“We're not trying to be the referee of truth,” the company’s about page states. “Instead, LogicLens helps uncover the context, so you can decide for yourself without the spin."

Of course, AI is increasingly used for online analysis and content review, and LogicLens is no exception. LogicLens doesn't identify the AI models powering its service in its publicly available documentation, but AI is definitely the backbone of the system.

According to LogicLens, it's using an AI system that's “Research-backed and custom designed to outperform general models like ChatGPT & even trained experts.” We’ll leave that up to anyone willing to give the tool a spin to decide, but one thing’s for certain: The world needs something.

Large language models and image generation tools are increasingly being used to generate internet content slop, and not all of it is as harmless as poorly made commercials for drop-shipped garbage: Some of it is being used to craft very convincing misinformation.

A 2024 study found that AI-generated misinformation was even more convincing than stuff crafted by humans - and that was two years ago. Just think how much worse it’s likely become since then.

To make matters worse, concerns have been raised about critical thinking skills being on the decline , potentially making it harder for people to identify falsehoods on the internet. AI users are reportedly less likely to admit they don’t know something, even though use of AI has been found in studies to l essen brain activity , leading to poorer retention of facts and worse performance on tests.

Is using more AI the solution to the problem? In an ideal world, we’d all just put the computers down and go touch grass, but we’re not in an ideal world: We’re living in the age of AI.

LogicLens is free but requires sign-up and restricts nonpaying users to 15 analyses a day and 100 over the course of a month. A $4.99 monthly subscription removes those analysis caps.  ®

item.title: Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down
item.description:
Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30.

Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. S ome 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names.

Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026."

Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ , users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images.

The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com , with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of.

It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will.

Mozilla told The Register : "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider."

It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere.

Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now.

Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

item.title: Email addresses used in European school bomb hoaxes spotted in old infostealer logs
item.description:
Two email addresses used to send bomb threats that disrupted thousands of Italian schools this week were found exposed in infostealer logs for over a year, experts say.

Researchers at Hudson Rock looked into the two university email addresses used to send the bomb threats. One, from Egypt’s Kafrelsheikh University, was scooped up by Vidar – a cybercrime tool that steals saved account credentials and passwords from an infected computer and leaks them to attackers – as far back as October 2021. The other, from Taiwan's Dayeh University, was found among the 284 million addresses included in the massive AlienTXTBASE infostealer dump , dated February 2025.

The experts said that the two addresses in infostealer logs do not strictly mean that those behind the bomb threats gained access to the accounts using the previous infostealer compromise.

However, it suggests that there was ample time for the universities and Microsoft, which both universities used for authentication, to take action against the accounts that they should have been aware were appearing in infostealer logs.

Modern threat intelligence has made infostealer logs highly visible.

"Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been investigated and secured," Hudson Rock said .

The researchers said that they would need access to details such as the email headers, and data from email providers, including sign-in events and audit records, that could show them more about who sent the email and from what session.

Understanding whether the sender authenticated into the account could rule out spoofing, but would not in itself provide proof that the sender used a corresponding password taken from an infostealer log, Hudson Rock noted. There are many ways to get around password-based authentication .

The researchers said that in any case where a credential is detected among infostealer logs, the organizations responsible for those accounts must contain them, revoke their access, rotate secrets, and go looking for suspicious activity.

"The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft," the researchers said.

"An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources."

The threats

Around 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools received fake bomb threat emails between November 11-12, although only around 390 of them evacuated their respective buildings.

The emails contained messaging such as "we will annihilate you," and "we will carry out genocide against Italians," and mention of a  "powerful explosive device… with a remote trigger."

Early reports suggested that the emails came from a Taiwanese email address and were signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan" – a fictitious state or region roughly mapping to "the land of Misogyny," with "vilayat" meaning an administrative region of the Ottoman Empire.

Various theories have been reported about the identity of the sender, ranging from a teacher based in the Philippines whose email was compromised to a Russia-backed disruption operation. Neither are confirmed. Russia denied any involvement.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Thursday evening that there was no credence to the emails, and that whoever was behind the coordinated hoax sought to invoke chaos across the country.

"To date, there is no evidence of a concrete danger," she said, ANSA reported. "These messages aren't intended to shock, they're intended to scare.

"Those who write them are primarily seeking our fear, wasted days, suspicion, and chaos. Investigators and the judiciary, along with their European colleagues, are working to determine who is behind them."

Schools in France, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland also received similar emails this week. None of the respective police forces believed the threats were legitimate.

Hundreds of schools across the Republic of Ireland received the emails, as did news organizations such as RTÉ, which evacuated its Donnybrook campus, disrupting scheduled programming.

Around 300 schools in Northern Ireland received bomb threats, although the PSNI said these were being treated as a hoax, and that the risk to the public was deemed low.

Likewise, Police Scotland confirmed around 1,000 schools were affected by the email campaign and that the threats weren’t believed to be credible.

In France, three school districts confirmed they received similar threats. Separately, domestic and international rail travel, including Eurostar services to London, were interrupted on Thursday following bomb threats made to Calais-Fréthun station.

The latest wave of threats follows similar happenings at other types of organizations in recent weeks, including airline operators, air traffic controllers, and blood banks.

At least 34 flights across various operators in Europe were affected earlier this month. Some were forced into unplanned landings, such as an Aer Lingus flight which pulled up to a French air base instead of its intended target of Rome.

Military fighter jets were also scrambled to escort others in Italian and Austrian airspace. ®

item.title: HPE debuts hybrid storage configs: Rising SSD costs hit supercomputing
item.description:
HPE is pitching high performance compute customers with hybrid configurations of its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems built for faster throughput, along with a Rack Management Controller that monitors cooling systems.

The hardware giant already supplies its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 in all-flash, all-disk, tiered and hybrid configurations, but - we're told - the latest combination offers up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack.

The E2000 line embeds the Lustre open-source parallel file system, and is generally intended to fit NVMe Gen 5 solid-state drive (SSD) building blocks.

For the refreshed hybrid configurations, HPE is combining SSDs with new 32 TB SAS-4 (24 Gb/s SAS) HDDs and new enclosures supporting 74 or 100 drives.

HPE says it'll deliver up to 116 GB/s of read throughput and 92 GB/s of write throughput per rack, with up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack for expansion to support the growing size of datasets in HPC, especially where sites are mixing AI and traditional simulation-style workloads.

One of the reasons behind these new hybrid configurations could be the ballooning cost of storage, caused by the relentless demand for AI infrastructure skewing the price of components such as memory and many other things. But prices for silicon-based NAND flash SSDs are growing faster than those of good old hard drives , as our colleagues at Blocks & Files reported.

HPE says that as demand for data-intensive workloads grows, prices for large SSDs have soared. The company claims the new hybrid configurations let research institutions and national laboratories spend less on storage and put that money toward compute node purchases, without giving up on the performance they need.

“When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements," said Trish Damkroger, HPE senior veep for HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions.

The latest hybrid configurations are expected to go on sale in early 2027.

HPE's other introduction is a Rack Management Controller, providing what HPE calls "intelligent liquid cooling” via real-time monitoring, leak detection and automated control features. It integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software to gather telemetry and provide control.

Several platform-specific versions will be offered, each tailored to different rack-scale systems. Support will launch with HPE's own Cray Supercomputing GX5000 infrastructure, naturally, with versions for Nvidia’s NVL72 and AMD’s Helion and Helios kit to follow.

The Rack Management Controller will be available for HPE’s kit in March 2027, with support for AMD and Nvidia expected to follow in June. ®

item.title: Microsoft outage gives customers a crash course in dependence on Redmond
item.description:
Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study.

Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope.

The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made ), and so on.

At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked.

Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems.

Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told The Register : "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today.

"This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs.

"When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped."

Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure."

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services."

This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as " permanently vulnerable ." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal.

And there are alternatives. Although perhaps not so extreme as the measures overheard by one vulture in a German shared workspace: "Germany's love of the fax machine – we are finally getting our chance to shine! Our British colleagues cannot email; we have reverted to the natural way of the fax."

What a time to be alive. ®

item.title: Graphon Labs raises $35M for persistent graphon intelligence memory it hopes will 'accelerate progress' towards AGI
item.description:
There are big claims and then there are BIG claims, and startup up Graphon Labs is making one of these; it says it is building the foundational infrastructure to help "accelerate progress towards AGI" and has raised $35 million to do it.

This plan is to build persistent intelligence to enable AI to continuously access, understand, remember, and build upon everything that came before, to help speed up work towards Artificial General Intelligence. It says that, as AI evolves from models that answer questions to agents that run around the clock, the ability to retain context, learn from experience, and accumulate knowledge over time becomes essential. The technology is built on graphons (graph functions), a mathematical framework for analyzing very large graphs, which Graphon Labs’ founders developed during their PhDs.

Arbaaz Khan , Graphon Labs co-founder and CEO, said: “The world is heading toward agents and physical systems that create and depend on more information than anyone has ever had to manage. In a world where we are moving to AI using computers, we need to fundamentally rethink how computers access data to pre-fill their context windows. The old way, using vector search, is like searching through the pages of a torn-up book. We take those pages and turn them into a connected map, unlocking seamless memory search.”

Graphon is a persistent intelligence platform for multimodal data. It ingests videos, images, audio, and documents using patent-pending technology, goes deep into the data to automatically build an ontology, and gives AI the context it needs.

It says vector search sees points, cutting our data into chunks, turning each one into a point, and returning the nearest few. Everything between the points (the reasons, the sequence, the relations) is gone. Graph RAG scores a chunk plus its neighbors, and is still limited.

Graphon builds one large graph of your data, then fits a graphon to it: the limit object of that graph, a single function that maps the topology of the full graph. A graphon is the continuous limit of a graph: one smooth function over all of your data instead of a pile of points. Nothing between the points is lost.

The other founders are CTO Clark Zhang and COO Deepak Mishra and the company was started up in July 2025 in San Francisco. The $35 million comes in an A-round led by RRE Ventures, with participation from HP, Energy Impact Partners, Hitachi Ventures, and Gaia VC. It follows an $8.3 million seed round. The graphon technology is derived from PhD research at the GRASP (General Robotics, Automation, Sensing and Perception ) Lab within the School of Engineering and Applied Sciences at the University of Pennsylvania.

The founders say their technology rethinks each layer of the stack, across storage, search, retrieval, reasoning, and memory. The result preserves what an agent knows, what it has done, what changed, and what happened as a result, with relationships, sources, and timing intact. It also cuts the compute time it takes to represent and reason across enormous amounts of information.

Graphon Labs says it’s building an intelligence architecture that scales from the enterprise to the individual. The goal is for it to sit beneath agents wherever intelligence needs to know, reason, act, remember, and learn. There are three products:

  • Graphon Enterprise: secure, governed memory across enterprise data across all modalities, so agents and teams can search and reason over it, deployed on hosted, Graphon-managed VPC, customer-managed VPC or on-prem infrastructure

  • Graphon Developer: builders can build over any data or modality without recreating the context stack

  • Graphon On-Device Memory: private, persistent multimodal intelligence on phones, laptops, cameras, wearables, and other devices

Their technology achieved the highest accuracy among evaluated systems on three leading benchmarks for long-term context: LoCoMo, ConvoMem and ATM-Bench . On LoCoMo, Graphon scored 93.9 percent accuracy using 58 percent fewer tokens than loading the full conversation into the model. On ConvoMem, it achieved 90.2 percent accuracy with 95 percent fewer tokens. On ATM-Bench, a benchmark from researchers at the University of Cambridge testing question answering across video, audio, images and text, Graphon scored 81.7 percent, 5.0 percentage points ahead of the next system on the public leaderboard. LoCoMo and ConvoMem comparisons use baseline results published by Databricks.

Initial users include the San Francisco 49ers and Hitachi Rail.

Khan added: "This funding takes us from early experimentation to scaled enterprise deployments, opens our infrastructure to developers, accelerates our research, and brings Persistent Intelligence on-device. Those are steps toward a bigger goal. When intelligence becomes lossless and continuous, it compounds, it improves faster, and eventually superintelligence becomes available to everyone. We'll measure our success by whether we build the infrastructure that gets intelligence to its next stage and make it available to all.”

item.title: HPE's hybrid Cray E2000 supercomputing storage hustler
item.description:
HPE says it has created the world’s fastest hybrid supercomputing storage with a hybrid SSD+HDD Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 array.

The E2000 is a Lustre file system-based offering available in all-flash, all-disk, hybrid SSD+HDD and tiered SSD+HDD configurations. The new hybrid configurations of the E2000 combine SSDs with 32-terabyte SAS-4 HDD, up from the 24 TB drives used previously, and SAS-4 HDD enclosures, supporting 74 or 100 drives. It's a response to higher NAND and SSD prices, which have risen 7x in the past 12 months according to HPE.

Trish Damkroger, SVP and GM for HPE’s HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions, said: “When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements. Our comprehensive portfolio, which now includes a world-leading hybrid supercomputing storage option, delivers powerful capabilities to scale, while maximizing capacity and optimizing costs.”

The Cray storage range consists of the C500 for smaller clusters, E1000 and E2000 for large supercomputers, and the K3000 for extreme systems, often paired with E2000). They run the Lustre or DAOS parallel file systems.

The E2000 is made up of building blocks, starting with a pair of System Management Units (SMU) with with SSDs to hold configuration and logging data. It then has MetaData Units (MDU) to store and manage global Lustre metadata. Each MDU contains a pair of Lustre metadata servers (MDS) and flash-based metadata targets (MDTs). An MDU is populated with 32 SSDs split into two partitions.

The actual data is held in Scalable Storage Units for disk (SSU-D) or flash (SSU-F) which provide Lustre I/O data services and network request handling for the file system. They contains Lustre object storage servers (OSS), each configured with object storage target (OSTs) to store and retrieve the portions of the file system data that are committed to it.

The new configuration provides:

  • Improved storage economics: Customers can match storage performance to processing requirements, while spending 82 percent less than they would on a comparable all-flash system.

  • More capacity, same data center footprint: Creating up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack, helping customers support growing datasets without expanding rack space.

  • High read-and-write performance: Delivering up to 116 GB per second of read throughput and 92 GB per second of write throughput per rack, enabling storage to better match the needs of HPC.

  • Up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack versus the next hybrid competitor, meaning DDN.

Regarding the storage economics, HPE says the lower acquisition cost is based on street pricing of 15 PB usable capacity meeting Nvidia specs for a 1,024-GPU cluster.

HPE has also introduced a new Rack Management Controller which will initially support Cray Supercomputing GX5000 systems, with future extensions for AMD and Nvidia rack-scale systems. It integrates with the HPE Supercomputing Management Software suite, including Foundation for infrastructure management, Composable for resource sharing, and Observability for operational monitoring. The integration shares rack-level telemetry and control capabilities, improving visibility and making it easier to operate and expand large, liquid-cooled HPC and AI environments.

Availability for the new hybrid configurations of HPE Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 is planned for early 2027. The Rack Management Controller for HPE Cray Supercomputing GX systems and the Supercomputing Management Software suite will be available in March 2027. Support for AMD and Nvidia rack-scale systems will follow in June 2027.

Get a look at the E2000 specifications here .

item.title: Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload
item.description:
Arm's Lorenzo Stoakes isn't quitting Linux kernel development, though he's stepping back from some of the patch-review work he used to handle.

Stoakes is a principal software engineer at Arm and he's a busy chap. Aside from writing the forthcoming book The Linux Memory Manager , in his CV [PDF], he says:

"I hold four maintainerships: memory mapping, memory mapping (locking), memory mapping (madvise) – essentially the entirety of the userland API to memory management – and the reverse mapping which connects physical to virtual memory."

Even so, he plans to soon be doing a little less. Earlier this week he posted an email to the Linux kernel mailing list to say that he was planning to drop some of his workload.

He explained:

"Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain. […] Apologies for doing this, but given the current trends I'd like to do something to make my inbox a little more manageable."

As it happens, this came just the day after the Paramount Penguin himself said that he saw signs that the AI patch tide was "starting to turn."

Stoakes told The Register :

"I am retaining my maintainerships and have no plans on giving those up, I just want my inbox to be less horrendous.

"And yeah, AI is part of the reason; in general, it's gone from 'once a week' to 'daily' to 'half of what I see in review'.

"But the AI wave is hitting [memory management] across the board, really."

He added:

"I have a habit of burning myself out over weekends and evenings – you can see my involvement on a thread talking about that here - which gives you a sense of my views if you read back through that thread."

At the Open Source Summit last month, the Reg FOSS desk joined the "Ask the Expert" session with Greg Kroah-Hartman , and he too expressed worrying sentiments:

"The onslaught of the LLM-generated patches… we don't have enough people to review them all… We need more reviewers. We don't have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years."

Kroah-Hartman also said:

"I want to go down to two Long Term Support releases – four, maximum. Six is too many. We're too busy. We don't have the manpower. It’s crazy."

On Red Hat's model of offering 10 years of support for products with a given version of the kernel:

"Debian does it right. Debian and Yocto run the world. I've argued for years that the RHEL and SLES model is broken. That's why I don't work for SUSE any more." ®

item.title: Startup Edelbyte has $70 million to develop big data analytics for AI agents
item.description:
Israeli startup Edelbyte is developing big data analytics for AI Agents and has raised $70 million in seed and A-round funding for the work.

Why do agents need big data analytics reinvented? Edelbyte says AI agents ask more questions, in unexpected ways, across more data than humans. Its product is built for both the unpredictability and the scale of agent needs. A built-in knowledge base gives agents the context they need, so they find the right answer faster. The company says that it aims to make real-time performance, meaning less than 100 ms, practical and cost-efficient at a hundreds of petabytes scale.

The cost part is $0.01/GB ingested data with full indexes. Its software provides a single platform providing search, analytical queries, vector, graph, geospatial and more with no need to stitch separate databases together. The software can run on-premises, in any cloud, public or sovereign, or be self-hosted. There is a unified query engine and queries are federated.

Edelbyte was founded by a foursome who worked on Azure Data Explorer (ADX), Microsoft’s fully managed big-data analytics service. Its internal development name was Kusto with a Kusto Query Language (KQL), and it provides real-time analysis of streaming, log, time-series, and telemetry data.

The four are:

  • Avner Aharoni - CEO,

  • Alexander Sloutsky - VP Engineering,

  • Evgeney Ryzhyk - CTO

  • Yoni Leibowitz - VP of platform engineering

The $70 million investment was led by Sequoia and Quiet Capital, with participation from Greenoaks and Swish Ventures.

It’s developing its technology with four early customers in the Fortune 500 area and petabyte-level deployments. Edelbyte will compete on the basis of speed and affordability against established players such as ClickHouse, Databricks, IBM, Microsoft, Oracle and Snowflake. Databricks is very aware of agents wanting to access and analyze the data it holds, with an acquisition strategy at work.

Edelbyte reckons that a having purpose-built, agent-access focussed engine is better than extending existing analytical systems intended originally for human scale and speed access. To coin a phrase, build it and the customers will come.

item.title: Neo4j’s rusty in-memory AI Agent graph database
item.description:
Graph database supplier Neo4j’s Relate is an in-memory database built in Rust for AI Agents and Agentic Systems.

Relate brings multihop reasoning capabilities and GraphRAG to AI agents for more accurate results and fewer hallucinations. It’s engineered specifically for the execution loops of autonomous agents, natively auto-detecting agent harnesses and returning structured errors equipped with explicit retryable flags. These flags enable agents to handle exceptions and self-correct without custom parsing logic. Relate enforces a row cap combined with an in-band truncation marker to prevent context window saturation during large retrievals. This constraint ensures agents receive bounded and predictable payloads.

Sudhir Hasbe, president of technology and CPO at Neo4j, said: "Relate is the ultimate agent-native database. Built in Rust for maximum speed and efficiency, it acts as a lightweight, in-memory store with highly durable disk storage, when needed, that can run anywhere. From seamless agent connectivity via MCP to multi-hop reasoning through full Cypher support, Relate provides a unique out-of-the-box solution designed to run in-process for agent sandboxes and agent memory as well as on mobile or edge devices.”

Cypher refers to the openCypher query language specification and implements the large majority of the newer ISO GQL (Graph Query Language) standard. Neo4j has been evolving Cypher toward GQL

Neo4j cites Gartner projections in Forecast Analysis: Agentic AI in DBMS, Worldwide, 2026 (June 2026) , saying that: “machine users will surpass human and AI assistant usage by 2029, reaching 75 percent of DBMS workloads, up from 10 percent in 2025.” It claims early enterprise adoption focused on simple conversational AI assistants for information retrieval and synthesis, but now budgets and workloads are shifting toward autonomous systems that can independently plan, execute and coordinate multistep operations.

It says the impact of AI agents/machine users will be far reaching, creating a new class of resource consumers -AI agents - that are becoming the primary users of databases and generating 10 to 100 times more interactions than humans and skyrocketing concurrent user loads

Relate can run anywhere and is built from the ground up as a lightning-fast, in-memory database engineered specifically for the agent paradigm. Neo4j says that, with Relate, AI coding agents can create a database and start building applications in milliseconds.

It delivers sub-millisecond reads in memory to handle the high-frequency read/write cycles of agentic workloads. A single Cypher statement can search by vector similarity and execute graph traversals simultaneously. The database maintains strict transactional integrity using an in-memory engine with an optional fsync'd write-ahead log for durable stores. It provides native options to flush state to disk for long-term persistence. Relate is 100 percent openCypher and more than 97 percent GQL compliant out of the box.

Relate deploys seamlessly across Jupyter notebooks, web browsers, software containers, and edge devices, and runs natively wherever agents are at work. The database ships with built-in agent connectivity via a Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server and a dedicated CLI for direct execution. Relate also exposes Bolt and HTTP Query API v2 endpoints to provide drop-in support for existing graph drivers, orchestration frameworks, and standard developer tooling.

Relate is open source software under the Apache 2.0 license, and is available now from here .

Bootnote

There are other in-memory databases built for AI agents:

  • ArcadeDB (embedded mode) is a multi-model database (property graph + document + key-value + more) that can run fully embedded / in-process.Memgraph is shipping a high-performance open-source in-memory graph database written in C/C++ and designed for GraphRAG, AI memory, agentic AI, and real-time graph analytics.

  • FalkorDB is an in-memory graph database (sparse-matrix / GraphBLAS-based engine) focused on low-latency multi-hop queries for AI agents, knowledge graphs, and GraphRAG.

  • Redis/Valkey (including Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey) is an ultra-low-latency in-memory key-value store that’s widely used as the short-term/working-memory layer for agents (session state, conversation buffers, and semantic caching.

Suggested positioning:

  • Relate - lightweight embedded graph store that agents can start themselves.

  • Memgraph - high-performance real-time graph analytics and AI context

  • FalkorDB - low-latency GraphRAG/multi-tenant agent memory.

  • Redis/Valkey - simple ultra-fast short-term state or vector cache.

item.title: Most affairs don't matter except to the people involved. Ex- Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world
item.description:
It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway.

The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed.

He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy!

In the aftermath, Nvidia's  CFO, Colette Kress, was appointed interim CEO. She won't, I suspect, be in the job for long. CFOs are not CEOs. The jobs aren't remotely the same.  In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang.

These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS.

That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999 , which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today.

That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA . This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing.

Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America , the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. First, they were in a state of shock. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. The second was that every month, Huang held an all-hands meeting where, instead of a per-forma corporate pep rally, he answered questions from everyone and gave them real answers. He knew his technology well and actually led his company instead of just impressing gullible stock buyers.

Nvidia can't replace him. It really can't. I'm reminded of when John Sculley forced Steve Jobs out at Apple in 1985. If you're not old enough to remember, Apple did fine for a while, but then by the mid-90s, it lost its way. Apple got its mojo back, and started its rise to being one of the world's top companies only after Jobs came back in 1996 .

The big difference, of course, is that Huang's not coming back. I heard many people say that Huang was "too big to fail." True, morality no longer matters much in the US – see Trump's kleptocracy – but this is different. Huang betrayed not just his wife, but his board, employees, and stockholders. If, as some suspect, the board knew full well what was going on, they should be tossed out too, but that's a story for another day.

Oh, and as for Trump's suggestions that Apple's former CEO Tim Cook should become Nvidia's CEO? Give me a break.

Now the question of the day is: how can Nvidia recover from this blow? I don't think it can. I used to say that I didn't know where the AI companies were going, but I was sure that so long as capital kept flowing into Big AI, Nvidia was the one company you could count on that would make money . I think I was wrong.

What does that mean? In the short term, Nvidia stock, after dropping 14 percent in early trading on Thursday, is down "only" five percent. Despite all the Sturm und Drang over Huang's departure, the NASDAQ is actually, when I wrote this, up. Even Nvidia's bonds are holding steady .

Amazon and Google, which have their own horses in the AI TPU races, are hoping, of course, that Nvidia's misfortune will help them lever open the AI hardware market. In these early hours, I don't see that happening.

Frankly, I'm amazed at how stockowners are shaking off Huang's resignation. The AI fever dream, for now, is continuing unabated.

That said, can this go on? This irrational exuberance rests on the belief that, no matter what happens, AI will continue to rule the stock market. Eventually, though, the bubble may pop, and that could put some strain on the global economy. For now, people are ignoring how bad this blow is, or perhaps they're not aware of it.

In a few years, I expect Huang's affair will be seen as the first needle in the AI bubble. ®

item.title: Oh my Word! Microsoft retires compatibility options, because who needs layouts to stay put
item.description:
Microsoft is retiring some legacy layout settings in Word, potentially rearranging documents created or last saved in Word 2010 or earlier.

"Affected documents may show layout differences, such as text reflow, changes in spacing or page count, or images and shapes moving to another page," the Windows biz said .

The advice, if silly little things like page layout in a document matter, is to "consider exporting it to PDF before the change."

Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout. Newer features are switched off while the document is open this way. Users can convert the document to unlock newer features, although people using older versions of Word may then have difficulty editing parts of it.

Microsoft has not identified the individual settings being retired, saying only: "We are retiring a set of compatibility options in Microsoft Word (desktop app) for documents in Compatibility Mode." The reason? "To simplify how Word handles document layout and provide a more consistent experience across platforms."

Administrators may therefore want to check older templates, forms, and other documents whose pagination needs to stay put.

The change is due to begin rolling out in the Windows version of Word from December 2026 and be completed by January 2027. The Mac version will follow in early 2027.

Microsoft Word is more than 40 years old, and its first Windows version was released as the 1980s drew to a close. The word processor has evolved over the decades and is a mainstay of Microsoft's productivity suite.

Compatibility Mode helps keep older documents from having their layouts abruptly borked the way Word does so well . Losing some of those safeguards could give administrators a fresh batch of "what the heck has happened to this document?" tickets as the change rolls out. ®

item.title: Quantum Systems drones back in the air after malware scare
item.description:
Quantum Systems says its drones are flying again with Germany's military after a cyberattack prompted a precautionary grounding.

The company says it spotted the attack at the end of October and reported it to the relevant authorities, but disclosed few details about the intrusion.

"The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday.

"Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems' unmanned systems for the end users and the operators."

It added that other players in the European defense industry, and those who support Ukraine's military efforts, have faced "persistent cyberattacks for years."

The Bundeswehr grounded its Quantum Systems drones after malware was detected in an update to QBase, the company's QBase ground-control software, Der Spiegel reported, citing unnamed sources. QBase lets operators plan missions, monitor flights, and process data from the ground.

The malicious update reportedly reached servers belonging to the German military and other customers, but did not directly infect the drones.

"The fleet is operating normally around the globe – including Germany and the Bundeswehr," Quantum Systems told Reuters . "The Bundeswehr was the only customer to ground their systems as a precaution."

A spokesperson for Germany's defense ministry declined to comment on the attack or the reported details. The Register asked Quantum Systems for further details.

Founded in 2015, Quantum Systems has been providing drones to the Ukrainian war effort for years.

Last month, Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced funding for "several tens of thousands" of the company's interceptor drones as part of Germany's winter aid package. The new drones will be built in Ukraine and support interceptor systems already in use on the front lines.

Quantum Systems announced a $1.2 billion Series D funding round in July, valuing the company at around $8 billion. ®

item.title: Palantir adds three UK police forces to its beat with £10.1M deal
item.description:
Three UK police forces led by Cambridgeshire Constabulary have awarded Palantir a £10.1 million contract after London Mayor Sadiq Khan blocked a separate deal with the Metropolitan Police.

The five-year agreement covers Bedfordshire Police, Cambridgeshire Constabulary, and Hertfordshire Constabulary, despite warnings from campaigners and politicians about dependence on the supplier.

A contract award notice says the east of England police forces expect the Palantir platform to provide "an enterprise-wide data integration and analytics capability, enabling the secure ingestion, linking, and analysis of data from multiple systems and sources across the policing environment." The contract runs until October 2031, with the estimated value covering all three forces.

News of the award coincided with revelations that former Metropolitan Police commissioner Dame Cressida Dick has worked as a paid adviser to Palantir since September 2025.

A Palantir spokesperson told the Bureau of Investigative Journalism : "Dame Cressida is advising us on how our software could help improve the delivery of services in the public sector, drawing on more than 40 years of public service in a variety of roles."

Dick said her role was limited to advising on how such products could assist public services. She said she had never lobbied or advocated for Palantir, or introduced the company to her contacts.

Dick led the Metropolitan Police, the UK's largest force, between 2017 and 2022. She left after Khan said he had lost confidence in her. She later said she was " intimidated " into leaving.

Separately, Khan stepped in to block the Met from awarding a £50 million contract to Palantir. His office cited serious concerns about the procurement process. Palantir later sued the Met, but the case was settled in October.

The new police contract award follows a report from MPs warning of vendor lock-in to US suppliers, including Palantir. It said : "Our view that Palantir's increasing presence across the public sector represents an unacceptable point of weakness is not ideologically motivated or driven by concerns about the quality of their products.

"The government should retain the ability to pick and choose individual suppliers and safeguard against the risk of vendor lock-in and debilitating dependencies, particularly in areas of critical national importance such as healthcare and national security infrastructure." ®

item.title: BOFH: The best way to stop an idea spreading is a controlled burn
item.description:
Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach...

And look, the Boss has his office door open!

C L E A R A N C E T O L A N D !

...

The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open.

His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us.

And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas.

"AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop.

He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town.

...

"For the security system," the Boss teases.

I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same.

The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea.

>clickety< >tap<

"Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed."

>tappity<

"And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too."

"It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to.

"A virus?!" the Boss gasps.

"I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing.

...

So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him.

Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow...

>tappity< >tap< >tap< >clickety<

On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously.

>tappity< >tap<

The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight.

On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling.

>bip< >bip< >bip< >biiiiiiip<

>ring<

"Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback.

"It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!"

Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard.

"What do I do?" the Boss gasps.

"It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!"

"I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks.

DAMMIT!

>tappity< >click< >tap< >tap<

Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device...

The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan.

...two hours later...

"So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden.

"Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor."

"It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. Our ideas spark innovation."

"It looks like there was some as-yet-unknown accelerant used."

"Really? Was it... enthusiasm?" I ask.

"No, more like lighter fluid."

"Oh," I say, thinking of the smokers the PFY occasionally chats to outside at the skip. "Well, we may never know."

"Don't you have some sort of AI surveillance system?" he asks.

"Sadly, that was the first thing to go," I lie.

...Later, in Mission Control...

"So, in review," the PFY says. "We shut down a couple of switches, put the building in night mode, trashed a laptop and a mobile phone, then set fire to the building."

"Yes."

"Simply to stop a dumb idea?"

"Yes."

"And the funny thing is, I took a look at his scribblings – and it wasn't all that bad."

"Really?" I ask, reaching for the isopropyl and a lighter, just in case it's contagious.
